query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled uniaxial tensile strain during post‐deposition annealing of single‐phase fcc FeCoNi thin films will induce a directional lattice distortion and local chemical ordering toward a lower-symmetry (e.g. partially L10‐like) state, thereby significantly enhancing magnetocrystalline anisotropy and increasing the coercivity well above 100 Oe.
generation.material_initial_state: Single‐phase fcc FeCoNi thin films (or closely related HEA derivatives) deposited on standard substrates, exhibiting high saturation magnetization and coercivity below ~100 Oe.
generation.intervention: Introduce a uniaxial tensile stress (via substrate bending or a mechanically flexible substrate setup) during the rapid thermal annealing process.
generation.conditions: Thin films sputtered on flexible or pre-strained substrates; rapid thermal annealing (e.g. 15–30 s RTA) performed under an applied uniaxial tensile load in an inert atmosphere; compositional range kept near equiatomic FeCoNi.
generation.structural_mediator: The uniaxial stress causes anisotropic lattice distortion that reduces the otherwise cubic symmetry and promotes directional chemical ordering at the atomic scale (potentially nucleating local L10-like motifs) without triggering multiphase separations or significant microstructural defects.
generation.mechanism: By breaking the cubic symmetry during annealing, the strain favors a more anisotropic lattice configuration. This anisotropy boosts the magnetocrystalline anisotropy energy, which impedes domain wall motion and thus leads to a substantial increase in coercivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally annealed films, the strained-annealed films will exhibit a significantly higher coercive field (potentially an order-of-magnitude or more increase, e.g. from <100 Oe to >300 Oe) while retaining a high saturation magnetization.
generation.baseline: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi films processed by standard deposition and RTA without externally applied strain, showing coercivities typically below 100 Oe.
generation.boundary: The study is limited to thin-film configurations where a uniaxial tensile load can be applied during annealing. The intervention is constrained to FeCoNi-based compositions near equiatomic ratios and to post-deposition thermal treatments under controlled conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence (PMC11426066::web::010::results_and_discussion) shows that RTA-induced lattice strain and induced chemical order can boost coercivity and other studies (PMC9685441::web::031::low_coercivity_analysis) link microstructural distortions to domain wall pinning, it is uncertain how effectively deliberately applied uniaxial tensile strain during annealing will promote the desired low-symmetry ordering in a single-phase fcc system.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of single-phase fcc FeCoNi thin films: one set processed by standard RTA and another processed by RTA under an applied uniaxial tensile strain (using a flexible substrate setup). Perform magnetic characterization (e.g. via vibrating sample magnetometry) and structural analysis (using XRD and TEM) to assess lattice symmetry and ordering.
measurements: Coercive field (Hc) via hysteresis loop measurements
X-ray diffraction patterns to detect changes in lattice symmetry/order
TEM to observe directional lattice distortions or emerging ordering motifs
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the strained-annealed films do not show a statistically significant increase in coercivity (for example, an increase by at least a factor of 1.5 to an order-of-magnitude relative to the control) or if structural analyses do not reveal any evidence of induced anisotropic lattice distortion or low-symmetry ordering, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The 1–2 orders of magnitude coercivity increase in RTA‐treated samples, compared to the as‐grown ones, suggests the emergence of sizeable magnetic anisotropy in the film. The fact that the continuous 15s RTA sample (Figure 1b) exhibits a 350 Oe coercivity, indicates that the dewetting process and film morphology evolution in some of the samples are not essential to the significant coercivity enhancement. Previous studies on bulk FeCoNiMnCu solid solutions have not found appreciable magnetic anisotropy ascribed to the disordered phase.[ ,  ] Hard magnetic properties in some solid solutions have been attributed to the magnetocrystalline or shape anisotropy of a secondary phase, however, studies of bulk phase‐separated FeCoNiMnCu have not shown large coercivity of the order presented here.[  ] In the present RTA‐treated samples, likely the anisotropic strain has induced lattice and grain distortions or directional chemical order, different from those in bulk systems, and stabilized sizable magnetic anisotropy, similar to that in RTA‐assisted synthesis of L10 FeCuPt.[ ,  ]

The coercivity increases when the domain wall movement is impeded by the microstructural discontinuities and sharp gradients.[  ] Therefore, the abundant microcracks in the CoCrFeNithin film would form a discontinuous interface for the magnetic flux, change the magnetic field distribution, and increase the leakage magnetic field above the cracks.[  ] Moreover, the microcracks can reinforce the pinning effect of the domain walls. Hence, the coercivity of the CoCrFeNithin film is larger than that of the CoCrFeNithick film. To eliminate the influence of the defects on the coercivity, we analyzed the relationship between the coercivity and the microstructure of the films without microcracks. According to the technical magnetization theory,[  ] H C is mainly related to the defect‐induced irreversible movement of the domain walls as well as the irreversible rotation of the magnetic moments, which are influenced by the magnetic anisotropy. Nanocrystalline soft magnetic materials exhibit a single domain structure owing to the small crystal grain sizes, and there is no domain‐wall movement during the magnetization‐reversal process.
